topic: Research: Apple Foundation Models Dynamic Profiles: Multi-Agent iOS Workflows (2026)

key_points: Apple positions Dynamic Profiles as Foundation Models primitives for dynamic context and agentic workflows.
The session covers declaring a dynamic profile, dynamic instructions, configuring models per phase, transcript/history transforms, lifecycle modifiers, and orchestration patterns.
Important implementation angle: baton-pass and phone-a-friend orchestration are first-party patterns for multi-agent app flows.

Apple frames the 2026 Foundation Models release around broader model access: new on-device model, image understanding, Private Cloud Compute, third-party model abstraction, system tools, Dynamic Profiles, evaluations, fm CLI, Python SDK, and open source plans.
Dynamic Profiles are introduced as a declarative API for agentic apps inside a single LanguageModelSession.
Useful differentiator for our article: connect Dynamic Profiles to model routing, evaluation, and production fallback strategy rather than treating them as only a Swift syntax feature.
Explains the practical problem Dynamic Profiles solve: switching model, instructions, and tools mid-session without manually rebuilding transcript context.
Uses a developer-friendly narrative around one session, multiple model personalities, and zero context loss.
Covers a basic DynamicProfile protocol example and recommends Apple sessions 241 and 242 for deeper implementation.
Frames Dynamic Profiles as an agent framework hidden inside one LanguageModelSession.
Shows an app-state-driven pattern where different modes use different instructions, tools, models, and generation options while preserving conversation history.
Highlights FoundationModelsUtilities history modifiers and notes that beta API names may change before final release.
Connects Dynamic Profiles to the new LanguageModel abstraction and third-party provider support such as Claude.
Explains the pre-2026 pain point: developers had to leave Foundation Models and integrate vendor APIs separately when they needed a non-Apple model.
Adds production/security angles, including proxying third-party credentials and using App Attest for cloud-model calls.

stats.fact: Apple announced the Foundation Models framework now works as a single native Swift API for on-device models with image input, server models, custom skills, and Dynamic Profiles.

Developers in the App Store Small Business Program with fewer than 2 million total first-time App Store downloads can access next-generation Apple Foundation Models on Private Cloud Compute at no cloud API cost.

WWDC26 session 241 lists Dynamic Profiles for agentic apps, composing models/configurations, an Evaluations framework, the fm CLI, Python SDK, and open source/framework utilities as major Foundation Models updates.
Apple says the Private Cloud Compute language model has a 32,000-token context window and reasoning capability for more demanding tasks.

Apple's third-generation AFM family includes AFM 3 Core, a next-generation 3-billion-parameter dense on-device model, and AFM 3 Core Advanced, a 20-billion-parameter sparse on-device model that activates 1 to 4 billion parameters per request.
Apple states AFM 3 Cloud Pro powers demanding use cases such as agentic tool use and complex reasoning.
WWDC26 session 339 says Foundation Models can now be extended by implementing a LanguageModelExecutor, letting local or server-based models back a LanguageModelSession.

Apple's 2025 Foundation Models research described the original developer-facing on-device language model as approximately 3B parameters and emphasized guided generation, tool calling, and built-in safety guardrails.

angles: Dynamic Profiles are best explained as context-preserving model routing, not just multi-agent branding.
The core developer win is replacing manual transcript copying between LanguageModelSession instances with declarative profile selection inside one session.
The 2026 architecture lets an iOS app combine local privacy, PCC reasoning, and third-party models while keeping one Swift programming model.
Production apps should define profile boundaries by latency, privacy, cost, context-window pressure, and tool permissions.
The underrated piece is evaluation: multi-agent iOS workflows need tests for tool-call trajectories, model handoffs, and prompt/profile regressions.
A strong unique section should warn that Dynamic Profiles do not remove orchestration design; developers still need routing rules, fallbacks, observability, and privacy boundaries.
The free PCC tier for qualifying small developers changes the economics of mobile agent features, but third-party model calls still need a secure credential/proxy design.
